title: Mysterious detail in 1937 painting sparks time travel theories
excerpt: Mysterious detail in 1937 painting sparks time travel theories
content:
Fun

Express newspaper

14/09/2026 14:58

A painting created nearly 90 years ago has returned to the attention of the internet, after an unusual detail in it has once again sparked theories that it could be "proof" of time travel.

The 1937 work, titled "Mr Pynchon and the Settling of Springfield," depicts a 17th-century scene in which an indigenous man is seen holding an object that, for some social media users, strikingly resembles a smartphone.

The figure in the foreground holds a dark object with white or silver edges and looks at it in a way that today might be reminiscent of someone using a telephone.

This very detail has fueled speculation for years that the artist may have included an object "from the future" in the painting.

"This really looks like a phone," one online user commented, while another asked: "Is it an iPhone?"

Historians have a much simpler explanation.

Despite theories circulating on social media, historians believe the object is much more likely to be a mirror.

According to this interpretation, the indigenous man may have obtained the mirror as part of a trade with English settlers led by William Pynchon.

Mirrors were common trade goods at the time, and the position of the character in the painting – holding the object in front of him and gazing at it – is consistent with someone looking at his own reflection.

Historian Daniel Crown was among those who argued in 2017 that the mysterious object was simply a European mirror used in trade.

What does the painting actually represent?

The mural is the work of Italian-born artist Umberto Romano and is one of six murals created during the American "New Deal" program.

They depict the history of Springfield, Massachusetts, the town where Romano grew up.

The painting in question depicts William Pynchon, the founder of Springfield, during trade exchanges with indigenous populations, most likely members of the Pocumtuc tribe, around the 1630s.

People, animals, and various goods appear on stage, while the object resembling a telephone remains the element that has attracted the most attention in the modern era.

It is not the only case that has prompted such theories.

Romano's painting is just one of several historical works that conspiracy theorists have linked to time travel.

Another example is the 19th-century painting “The Expected One,” by Austrian artist Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller.

It shows a woman walking on a path and looking intently at a small object she is holding in both hands.

Historians believe the object is a book or a prayer book, but some internet users have pointed out that its posture resembles the way people walk today while looking at their phones.

Similar theories have been raised about an ancient Greek sculpture known as the "Grave Naiskos of an Enthroned Woman with an Attendant".

Some have claimed that the object shown in it resembles a laptop, even claiming that "USB ports" are visible on the side.

Archaeologists, however, reject such interpretations and explain the objects according to the context of the era in which they were created.

Viral claims about "travelers from the future"

In parallel with the resurgence of interest in the 1937 painting, interviews with people who claim, without providing evidence, to have traveled in time have also circulated on the internet.

One of them, a masked man who introduced himself as Alexander Smith, claimed to have been a member of the CIA in 1981 and to have been sent to the year 2118.

He also claimed that time travel technology has existed for decades and that it will become available to the public starting in 2028.

Smith went even further, claiming that that same year the US government would discover the existence of intelligent extraterrestrial beings.

No verifiable evidence has been presented for these statements.

Modern illusion or historical mystery?

Experts point out that people often interpret old works through the technology and experiences of the present.

An object that today may remind us of a smartphone may have had a completely different function at the time the work was created.

In the case of “Mr Pynchon and the Settling of Springfield,” the most accepted explanation remains that the object is a commercial mirror and not a modern device.

However, the visual similarity continues to make the painting one of those historical images that occasionally resurfaces on the internet and fuels unusual theories about time travel. /GazetaExpress/
